**Squared loss lets a few extreme residuals dominate the gradient.** Errors of 1 and 20 contribute 1 and 400 to squared loss. The larger error therefore receives 400 times the loss contribution, even if it arose from an unusual jump or a bad observation. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html)

Huber loss behaves quadratically near zero and linearly beyond a threshold. Its gradient stops growing proportionally with extreme error, reducing tail influence while retaining smooth behavior for ordinary residuals. That can improve robustness, but clipping the influence of genuine rare events may also hide risk important to the application.

**Other losses ask different questions.** Correlation losses emphasize cross-sectional association and ignore some scale information. A prediction vector multiplied by a positive constant has the same Pearson correlation but different probability or return calibration. Sharpe-inspired objectives combine average outcome and variability, yet can be unstable when estimated on small or unrepresentative batches.

Differentiable rank approximations add another approximation to the desired ordering metric. Compare objectives using forward validation, net outcomes after costs, tail behavior, and uncertainty. Do not choose a loss merely because its name resembles a preferred backtest statistic. The training objective, portfolio construction, and execution assumptions must together represent the intended decision problem.

**Technical details and references.**

Squared loss gives large residuals quadratic influence, so extreme returns can dominate training. Huber becomes linear beyond a threshold, reducing outlier influence while remaining smooth near zero. Correlation losses target cross-sectional ordering/association, and Sharpe-inspired objectives target return relative to volatility. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/model_evaluation.html)

$$L_\delta(e)=\begin{cases}e^2/2,&|e|\le\delta\\\delta(|e|-\delta/2),&|e|>\delta.\end{cases}$$

These objectives optimize different quantities. Correlation ignores absolute calibration and can be unstable in tiny batches; Sharpe losses can exploit noisy denominator estimates or ignore costs/tail risk. Differentiable rank approximations introduce their own smoothing bias. Evaluate net portfolio outcomes, robustness, and uncertainty with temporal validation; a training loss aligned with one backtest statistic is not a guarantee of live performance.
